title: The 250 Trail: Chicago — The Neighborhood Mosaic
hook: One city, 77 official pieces, each built by somebody who just got here. Eat the mosaic — Polish sausage to carnitas, dim sum to glögg — on the streets where the blues plugged in.
narrative: Chicago keeps its books in neighborhoods — 77 official community areas, mapped in the 1920s and barely changed since, each one a ledger of who arrived and what they built. This trail reads a few pages. Start at Maxwell Street, where a Macedonian immigrant named Jimmy Stefanovic bought his aunt's hot dog stand in 1939 and — by most tellings — invented the Maxwell Street Polish in 1943; the same market where bluesmen up from the Delta plugged into borrowed extension cords so the guitar could carry over the haggling. That corner is the whole city in miniature: everybody's food, everybody's music, volume up. From there, Pilsen — named by Czech immigrants for Plzeň, remade by Mexican families in the 1960s, home to a free-admission museum of Mexican art founded in 1982 by educators who pooled $900. Then Chinatown, planted at Cermak and Wentworth in 1912, where the On Leong Merchants Association raised its own building and made a neighborhood. Then Bronzeville, the Black Metropolis built by the Great Migration — more than 100,000 Black Chicagoans by 1920, and the sound they carried north still plays live every night. Finish where a Swedish tavern has poured since 1934 up in Andersonville — after a Ukrainian Village tasting counter that carried Filipino cooking to a Michelin star. No single stop is the point here. The mosaic is. Come hungry; it's a long, wide city.

stops.note: The mosaic's front door. Jimmy Stefanovic, a Macedonian immigrant, took over this Maxwell Street stand in 1939 and, by most tellings, invented the Maxwell Street Polish in 1943 — order it with grilled onions on the block where the blues went electric.
Pilsen was named by Czechs and remade by Mexican families, who built this museum from a $900 start in 1982 into the only Latino museum accredited by the American Alliance of Museums. Free, always.
The everyday backbone of 18th Street: slow-cooked carnitas by the pound, tortillas and salsa on the side. This is the Pilsen the museum celebrates, still open by 7am.
Dim sum carts rolling through the neighborhood Chinese merchants built for themselves after moving south to Cermak and Wentworth in 1912. Come early on weekends — the whole city shows up.
Bronzeville, where the Great Migration set the table. White tablecloths, fried chicken and catfish, and a Sunday brunch that has been a community institution for decades.

Buddy Guy arrived from Louisiana in September 1957, went three days hungry, and refused to pawn his guitar. His South Loop club keeps the migration's sound live on stage — catch his January residency if you can.

The mosaic's newest tile: Tim Flores and Genie Kwon's Ukrainian Village storefront became the world's first Michelin-starred Filipino restaurant. Kasama means 'together' in Tagalog — the trail's thesis on a plate. Daytime bakery counter, no reservation needed.
Andersonville's Swedish anchor — Simon Lundberg went from Prohibition speakeasy to licensed tavern in 1934, and the glögg still simmers every winter under the original woodwork.
End on Devon Avenue, the Pakistani and Indian main street that proves the mosaic never stops adding tiles. Green chili chicken and biryani, absurdly cheap, open until 4am.
